title: Ordered spectral separation
subtitle: G2 lecture 065000 · expanded companion
adaptation: Expanded, source-grounded mathematical companion: independent derivations, worked examples, vector MathTex, reusable diagrams. Spoken source unchanged.

slides.title: The problem and its setting
slides.eyebrow: G2 · 065000 · The problem and its setting
slides.lead: For the Sylvester equation A X minus X B equals C, disjoint spectra can guarantee a unique solution, but existence alone gives no quantitative bound on its norm.
body: An ordered positive gap between self-adjoint coefficient operators provides a much stronger conclusion. Suppose A and B are self-adjoint, and every spectral value of A lies at least delta above every spectral value of B, where delta is positive.

This is ordered spectral separation. Under that hypothesis, the solution of A X minus X B equals C can be written as an integral of decaying exponentials, and its operator norm is at most the norm of C divided by delta.
slides.takeaway: Ordered spectral separation provides exponential decay in one time direction.

slides.title: What ordered separation says
body: Put the spectrum of B entirely to the left. Leave an empty interval of positive length delta. Then put the spectrum of A to the right. For example, B may have eigenvalues zero and one, while A has eigenvalues three and five.
The smallest difference between an eigenvalue of A and an eigenvalue of B is two. So we can take delta equal to two. The condition is stronger than the assertion that the spectra do not overlap.
slides.takeaway: A common cut puts every eigenvalue of A above every eigenvalue of B.

slides.title: The scalar integral behind the proof
slides.eyebrow: G2 · 065000 · The scalar integral behind the proof
slides.lead: Take real numbers a and b with a greater than b.
body: Consider the scalar function of time that is the exponential of negative t times a minus b. As time increases, this function decays. Integrating from zero to infinity gives one divided by a minus b. We can prove it without quoting an integral table.

The derivative of the exponential of negative t times the difference is negative that difference times the same exponential. Divide by the difference and evaluate the antiderivative between zero and a large time T. The upper endpoint goes to zero, leaving the reciprocal.
slides.takeaway: The reciprocal spectral difference is an integral of a decaying scalar function.

slides.title: Two exponentials, one Sylvester solution
slides.eyebrow: G2 · 065000 · Two exponentials, one Sylvester solution
slides.lead: Integrating transported residuals produces the candidate solution.
body: For bounded self-adjoint A and B with A spectrally above B, form F(t)=e^(−tA)Ce^(tB). In diagonal coordinates its (i,j) coefficient is e^(−t(aᵢ−bⱼ))Cᵢⱼ.
Integrating from zero to infinity divides each coefficient by aᵢ−bⱼ. The operator integral expresses the same calculation without choosing eigenvectors.
slides.takeaway: The operator integral reproduces every spectral coefficient of the solution.

slides.title: Find a common spectral cut
slides.eyebrow: G2 · 065000 · Find a common spectral cut
slides.lead: Because the spectra are compact in the bounded self-adjoint setting, there is a real number c such that all spectral values of B are at most c, while all spectral values of A are at least c plus delta.
body: For our example, take c equal to one. B lies at or below one. A lies at or above three. Since delta is two, the required difference is exact. For nonnegative time, the norm of the exponential of negative t A is at most the exponential of negative t times c plus delta.
That is because the spectrum of the exponential consists of the exponentials of the original spectral values, and the largest such value corresponds to the smallest eigenvalue of A.
slides.takeaway: The spectral cut supplies one uniform decay rate for all blocks.

slides.title: Integrate the norm bound
slides.lead: Since delta is positive, the exponential of negative delta times t is integrable over nonnegative times.
body: Its integral is one over delta. The norm of an operator-valued integral is at most the integral of the operator norms. Therefore the norm of the proposed solution is at most the norm of C divided by delta.

This statement is independent of the dimension. Nothing in the decay estimate counts eigenvectors or matrix entries. It works on infinite-dimensional Hilbert spaces as long as A and B are bounded self-adjoint operators and the ordered separation holds. We also obtain convergence of the integral. The scalar exponential provides an integrable dominating function.
slides.takeaway: The integral norm is bounded by the scalar decay integral.

slides.title: Verify the equation by differentiation
slides.eyebrow: G2 · 065000 · Verify the equation by differentiation
slides.lead: Differentiate to verify the operator equation.
body: The derivative of F(t)=e^(−tA)Ce^(tB) is −AF(t)+F(t)B. Consequently A∫F−(∫F)B=−∫F′=F(0)−limₜ→∞F(t).
The ordered gap gives exponential decay, so the limit is zero and F(0)=C. This verifies AX−XB=C rather than only guessing the solution from scalar analogies.
slides.takeaway: Differentiation verifies the equation directly for bounded operators.

slides.title: A numerical check
slides.lead: Return to A diagonal with entries three and five and B diagonal with entries zero and one.
body: Let C be the two-by-two matrix whose entries are all one. Every coefficient of the solution is the corresponding coefficient of C divided by its spectral difference. The first row is one third and one half.

The second row is one fifth and one fourth. We can check the first row: multiplying by A gives one and three halves; multiplying on the right by B gives zero and one half; subtraction yields one and one.
slides.takeaway: A small diagonal example makes the integral formula checkable.

slides.title: Sharpness and reversed order
body: Take one-dimensional spaces. Let A multiply by delta, B multiply by zero, and C multiply by one. Then X multiplies by one over delta, so the bound is an equality. If the order is reversed, with A entirely below B, we can exchange the direction of time and the sign of the formula, or apply the result after swapping A and B.
The same norm estimate holds. What matters is consistent ordering, not which operator is above. Finally, be careful about hypotheses.
slides.takeaway: The constant one is sharp, and reversing the common order also works.

slides.title: Proof map: the ordered-gap theorem
slides.lead: The scalar Laplace transform becomes an operator-valued inverse.
body: Find a cut c separating σ(B) below from σ(A) above by δ. Then F(t)=e^(−tA)Ce^(tB) decays at rate δ, so X=∫₀∞F(t)dt exists and ||X||≤||C||/δ. Differentiating F verifies the Sylvester equation.
A one-dimensional example attains equality. The ordered hypothesis is the step that supplies simultaneous decay.
slides.takeaway: Spectral order, not mere distance, drives the constant-one semigroup proof.
